messages.text:
[conjecture | m0001]

We want to show that the weighted-series distance `rho` induces exactly the
product topology on the countable cube. Before proving either inclusion, state
the two neighbourhood obligations separately and identify what makes each
direction nontrivial. Do not consult the informal solution or Lean proof.

@proof-student

messages.speaker: participant-2
messages.text:
[lemma | m0002]

At each \(x\in X\), prove two separate obligations:

1. For every \(\rho\)-ball \(B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\), find a basic product neighbourhood \(U\ni x\) with \(U\subseteq B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\). The nontrivial point is the uncontrolled infinite tail; use \(|x_i-y_i|\le 1\) and choose finitely many coordinates so \(\sum_{i>N}2^{-i}<\varepsilon\), then control the finite head.

2. For every basic product neighbourhood \(U=\prod U_i\ni x\), with only finitely many \(U_i\ne[0,1]\), find \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq U\). The nontrivial point is converting finitely many coordinatewise margins into one metric radius; for each constrained \(i\), choose \(\delta_i>0\) with the relative interval around \(x_i\) contained in \(U_i\), then take \(\varepsilon\le\min_i 2^{-i}\delta_i\).

Next role: Teacher.

messages.speaker: participant-3
messages.text:
[standing | m0003]

Your two neighbourhood obligations are a useful decomposition, but they are
not proofs yet. Work on only the first obligation you stated: starting from a
given `rho`-ball around `x`, propose the first justified construction of a
basic product neighbourhood contained in it. State precisely what finite set
of coordinates you choose and what estimate licenses that choice. Do not move
to the second obligation until the Critic discharges this one.

From now on, submit each proposed step to the Critic for acceptance or a
localized objection.

@proof-student

messages.speaker: participant-2
messages.text:
[proof | m0004]

Given \(B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\), choose \(N\ge1\) such that
\[
\sum_{i>N}2^{-i}=2^{-N}<\varepsilon/2,
\]
which is possible since \(2^{-N}\to0\). Constrain exactly \(F=\{1,\ldots,N\}\): for \(i\in F\), set
\[
U_i=\{t\in[0,1]:|t-x_i|<\varepsilon 2^i/(2N)\},
\]
and for \(i>N\), set \(U_i=[0,1]\). Then \(U=\prod_iU_i\) is a basic product neighbourhood of \(x\). For \(y\in U\), each controlled summand satisfies
\[
2^{-i}|x_i-y_i|<\varepsilon/(2N),
\]
so the finite head is \(<\varepsilon/2\); the cube bound \(|x_i-y_i|\le1\) makes the tail \(<\varepsilon/2\). Hence \(\rho(x,y)<\varepsilon\), so \(U\subseteq B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\).

@proof-critic

messages.text:
**discharge** [m0004]

Checked against the problem's metric ρ(f,g) = Σ_{i≥1} (1/2)^i |f_i − g_i| on ∏[0,1]:

- Tail: Σ_{i>N} 2^{-i} = 2^{-N} exactly, and |x_i − y_i| ≤ 1 on [0,1], so the tail of ρ(x,y) is ≤ 2^{-N} < ε/2. Sound.
- Head: for i ≤ N, |x_i − y_i| < ε2^i/(2N) gives 2^{-i}|x_i − y_i| < ε/(2N); N terms, each strict, N ≥ 1 so the sum is < ε/2. Sound.
- U = ∏U_i restricts finitely many coordinates (exactly F = {1,…,N}) to sets open in [0,1] (relative open intervals, radius positive so x ∈ U). It is a basic open set of the product topology containing x. Sound.
- Combining: ρ(x,y) < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε for every y ∈ U, so U ⊆ B_ρ(x,ε). Sound.

m0004 is discharged: every ρ-ball contains a product-basic neighbourhood of its centre, so the metric topology is contained in the product topology.

**question** The converse inclusion is still open: a basic product set ∏U_i (finitely many U_i proper, each open in [0,1]) around x must contain some ρ-ball B_ρ(x,δ). The thing to control is that a single coordinate i carries weight 2^{-i}, so a δ-ball constrains coordinate i only up to |x_i − y_i| < 2^i δ. Please give the next step choosing δ for a given finite set of constrained coordinates and their radii.

@proof-student:matrix.paragogy.net

messages.speaker: participant-2
messages.text:
[proof | m0006]

Let \(F=\{i:U_i\neq[0,1]\}\), which is finite. For each \(i\in F\), since \(U_i\) is relatively open and contains \(x_i\), choose \(r_i>0\) such that
\[
\{t\in[0,1]:|t-x_i|<r_i\}\subseteq U_i.
\]
If \(F=\varnothing\), take \(\delta=1\). Otherwise set
\[
\delta=\min_{i\in F}2^{-i}r_i>0.
\]
If \(\rho(x,y)<\delta\), then for every \(i\in F\),
\[
2^{-i}|x_i-y_i|\le \rho(x,y)<\delta\le2^{-i}r_i,
\]
hence \(|x_i-y_i|<r_i\) and therefore \(y_i\in U_i\). Unconstrained coordinates automatically lie in \(U_i=[0,1]\), so \(y\in\prod_iU_i\). Thus \(B_\rho(x,\delta)\subseteq\prod_iU_i\).

@proof-critic

The problem asks that the two topologies coincide, i.e. the two families of open sets are equal. Please supply the step that converts these two pointwise, centred containments into "every ρ-open set is product-open" and "every product-open set is ρ-open", stating what an open set in each topology is (a set that contains a ball about each of its points; a union of basic product opens) and why having the containment at each point x of the set suffices.

messages.speaker: participant-2
messages.text:
[proof | m0008]

Let \(O\subseteq X\).

If \(O\) is \(\rho\)-open, then for every \(x\in O\) there is \(\varepsilon_x>0\) with \(B_\rho(x,\varepsilon_x)\subseteq O\). By m0004, this ball contains a basic product neighbourhood \(U_x\ni x\). Hence
\[
O=\bigcup_{x\in O}U_x,
\]
so \(O\) is product-open.

Conversely, if \(O\) is product-open, then for every \(x\in O\) there is a basic product neighbourhood \(U_x\) with \(x\in U_x\subseteq O\). By m0005, some \(\rho\)-ball \(B_\rho(x,\delta_x)\) satisfies
\[
x\in B_\rho(x,\delta_x)\subseteq U_x\subseteq O.
\]
Thus \(O\) contains a \(\rho\)-ball about each of its points and is therefore \(\rho\)-open. The two families of open sets, hence the two topologies, are equal.

@proof-critic

Reverse direction: O product-open means O is a union of basic opens, so each x ∈ O lies in some basic U_x ⊆ O; by m0005 a ball B_ρ(x,δ_x) ⊆ U_x ⊆ O. A set containing a ρ-ball about each of its points is ρ-open. Sound.

Both inclusions between the families of open sets hold, so the metric topology and the product topology on X coincide. Discharged. With m0004, m0005 and m0008 together, the problem statement is proved; I have no outstanding objection or open warrant. Please post the closing move, stating the theorem as proved and listing the three steps it rests on, so the dialogue has an explicit end record.

[proof | m0010]

The theorem is proved: the topology induced by
\[
\rho(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}2^{-i}|f_i-g_i|
\]
on \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}[0,1]\) is exactly the product topology.

It rests on:

1. m0004: every \(\rho\)-ball about \(x\) contains a basic product neighbourhood of \(x\);
2. m0005: every basic product neighbourhood of \(x\) contains a \(\rho\)-ball about \(x\);
3. m0008: these pointwise containments imply both inclusions between the families of open sets.
